# Investigative Report: Linking the Ronin Bridge and Harmony Horizon Bridge Thefts to Lazarus Group

## Executive assessment

The available evidence supports a strong public-attribution link between the March 2022 Ronin Bridge theft and the June 2022 Harmony Horizon Bridge theft. Both incidents were publicly attributed to Lazarus Group, a North Korea-backed state hacking organization. The Ronin attribution was reinforced by the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), which identified the relevant Ethereum address as belonging to Lazarus Group. The Harmony attribution was initially made by Elliptic through analysis of the laundering activity and was later confirmed publicly by the FBI. ([S1](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft); [S3](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

The link between the two cases is not based solely on the fact that both involved cross-chain bridges or North Korea. The available sources describe materially similar post-theft laundering behavior: movement of stolen assets through intermediary wallets; conversion of stablecoins or other assets into Ether; use of Tornado Cash in structured batches; cross-chain movement and asset conversion through decentralized finance services; and subsequent attempts to reach centralized exchanges or crypto-to-fiat cash-out points. ([S2](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/); [S3](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

The evidence is therefore most consistent with a common operational actor or organization—publicly identified as Lazarus Group—using a recurring laundering playbook against bridge-related cryptocurrency thefts. However, the supplied material does not provide complete wallet-address lists, transaction hashes, cryptographic indicators, or independently verifiable attribution data sufficient to identify individual operators or prove that every wallet in either laundering chain was controlled directly by the same human actors. The APT38 designation is also not independently established in the supplied sources; accordingly, this report treats “Lazarus Group/APT38” as a requested analytical association rather than a fact proven by the provided evidence.

## Sources and evidentiary scope

For clarity, the source identifiers used in this report are:

| Source ID | Publisher and date | Relevance |
|---|---|---|
| **S1** | Elliptic, May 9, 2023 | FBI confirmation of the Harmony Horizon attribution and description of Harmony laundering through Tornado Cash, Railgun, and exchanges |
| **S2** | Chainalysis, September 8, 2022 | Ronin theft, laundering typology, cross-chain laundering, and seizure of more than $30 million |
| **S3** | Elliptic, March 29, 2022, updated April 14, 2022 | Ronin theft, OFAC attribution to Lazarus Group, validator compromise, and early laundering evidence |

The supplied evidence consists primarily of public investigative and analytical reporting by Elliptic and Chainalysis. These are specialist blockchain-intelligence companies with direct visibility into on-chain activity, but their published accounts are not equivalent to a complete law-enforcement evidentiary file. Their attribution findings should therefore be distinguished from facts independently confirmed by a government authority.

## The Ronin Bridge theft

### Theft mechanics and scale

Ronin Network disclosed that 173,600 ETH and 25.5 million USDC had been stolen from its cross-chain bridge. Elliptic valued the assets at approximately $540 million at the time of the theft, while Chainalysis described the incident as a theft of more than $600 million, reflecting different valuation points and reporting contexts. Elliptic also stated that the assets were worth more than $615 million when the incident was discovered. ([S2](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/); [S3](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

According to the Ronin postmortem as summarized by Elliptic, the bridge required five of nine validator approvals for funds to move. The attacker obtained the private cryptographic keys associated with five validators, which was sufficient to authorize the fraudulent withdrawals. The postmortem characterized the incident as socially engineered rather than the result of a purely technical flaw. ([S3](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

Chainalysis described the same attack as involving access to five of nine validator keys, followed by two unauthorized withdrawals: 173,600 ETH and 25.5 million USDC. ([S2](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/))

### Public attribution

The Ronin theft was publicly attributed to Lazarus Group by OFAC. Elliptic reported that, on April 14, 2022, OFAC sanctioned the Ethereum address associated with the theft and identified its owner as Lazarus Group, described as a North Korean state hacking group. ([S3](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

This is the strongest attribution statement in the supplied evidence because it is presented as a government sanctions action rather than solely as a private-sector analytical assessment. Nevertheless, sanctions designation is an attribution and enforcement measure, not a technical disclosure of all underlying intelligence. The source material does not identify the individual persons who controlled the relevant keys or wallets.

## The Harmony Horizon Bridge theft

### Theft mechanics and scale

Elliptic reported that Harmony’s Horizon Bridge was exploited on June 24, 2022, for approximately $99.7 million, commonly described as a $100 million theft. The bridge serviced the Harmony blockchain and had previously attracted criticism because of its centralized validator and key-management structure. Elliptic assessed that this centralization made the bridge vulnerable to social-engineering attacks, which it characterized as a common attack vector for Lazarus Group. ([S1](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

The supplied material does not provide the exact technical exploit sequence or a list of the Horizon wallets. It does, however, provide post-theft transaction observations and a description of the laundering flow.

### Public attribution

Elliptic stated that it was the first organization to identify the Harmony theft as North Korean activity, based on similarities between the laundering patterns used after Harmony and those associated with earlier Lazarus operations, including the Ronin incident. Elliptic later reported that the FBI confirmed Lazarus Group was responsible for the Harmony theft. ([S1](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

Accordingly, the Harmony attribution has two evidentiary layers in the supplied sources:

1. **Private-sector assessment:** Elliptic identified similarities in transaction structuring and laundering behavior.
2. **Government confirmation:** The FBI subsequently confirmed the Lazarus attribution.

The FBI confirmation materially strengthens the connection between Harmony and Ronin because Ronin had already been publicly associated with Lazarus through OFAC. ([S1](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft); [S3](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

## Comparative laundering patterns

### Shared characteristics

The following table summarizes the common features reported for both thefts:

| Feature | Ronin Bridge | Harmony Horizon Bridge | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Public attribution | OFAC identified the relevant address as Lazarus Group | FBI confirmed Lazarus Group involvement | Strong common attribution |
| Initial asset handling | Stolen USDC was converted into ETH through decentralized exchanges | Funds were structured and routed through Tornado Cash | Conversion and obfuscation were central |
| Mixer use | Tornado Cash used in batches | Tornado Cash used programmatically and in structured transactions | Directly similar laundering behavior |
| Cross-chain activity | ETH bridged to BNB Chain, swapped for USDD, then bridged to BitTorrent Chain | Railgun used after Tornado Cash sanctions; deposits later reached exchanges | Both used DeFi and cross-chain mechanisms |
| Intermediary wallets | More than 12,000 addresses used in the laundering process, according to Chainalysis | Post-mixer withdrawals placed into several addresses and later restructured | Distributed wallet infrastructure |
| Exchange exposure | More than $30 million seized with industry and law-enforcement cooperation | Binance and Huobi reportedly blocked and seized a portion | Centralized exchanges were disruption points |

([S1](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft); [S2](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/); [S3](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

### Tornado Cash and structured transaction behavior

For Ronin, Elliptic reported that the stolen USDC was first exchanged for ETH through decentralized exchanges, which reduced exposure to token issuers capable of freezing stablecoins and avoided the KYC and AML controls of centralized exchanges. The attacker then sent approximately $16.7 million in ETH through three centralized exchanges before shifting toward Tornado Cash after the exchanges publicly indicated that they would cooperate with law enforcement. ([S3](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

Elliptic reported that approximately $80.3 million in Ronin-linked ETH had been sent through Tornado Cash by April 14, 2022, with another approximately $9.7 million held in intermediary wallets and apparently prepared for further laundering. At that point, approximately $433 million remained in the original attacker wallet, according to the source’s contemporaneous analysis. ([S3](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

For Harmony, Elliptic observed programmatic transaction structuring through Tornado Cash. It reported that the methods resembled those used in the Ronin laundering operation. Elliptic estimated that more than $555 million linked to the two hacks had passed through Tornado Cash: more than $468 million from Ronin and approximately $96 million from Harmony. ([S1](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

The numerical relationship is significant. The reported amounts are close to the total values of the respective thefts, suggesting that Tornado Cash was not incidental to either operation but a major component of the laundering strategy. The figures should nevertheless be treated as contemporaneous analytical estimates, not final audited recovery or loss totals.

### Shift toward cross-chain DeFi and Railgun

Chainalysis reported that, after OFAC sanctioned Tornado Cash, Lazarus Group moved away from the Ethereum mixer and used decentralized finance services to chain-hop and switch among multiple cryptocurrencies. One cited Ronin example involved bridging ETH from Ethereum to BNB Chain, swapping it for USDD, and bridging the resulting asset to the BitTorrent Chain. Chainalysis stated that hundreds of similar transactions were carried out across several blockchains. ([S2](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/))

Elliptic reported that Harmony-linked funds later entered Railgun, a privacy-focused DeFi protocol functioning similarly to a mixer. The activity began in January 2023, after the post-Tornado withdrawals had remained dormant in several addresses. Elliptic estimated that approximately 70% of Ether sent through Railgun to that date represented Harmony-hack funds. It argued that this unusually high concentration reduced the effectiveness of the mixing because the anonymity set was comparatively small. ([S1](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

This transition is analytically important. The two cases demonstrate continuity in the objective—obscuring the source of stolen assets—but adaptation in the means. Tornado Cash was used prominently before and around the time of sanctions; subsequent activity relied more heavily on cross-chain bridges, token swaps, and Railgun-like privacy infrastructure.

## Wallet evidence and limitations

The supplied sources contain meaningful wallet-level observations but do not reproduce the actual addresses. For Ronin, Elliptic reported an original attacker wallet holding approximately $433 million at the time of its April 14, 2022 analysis, intermediary wallets holding approximately $9.7 million, and addresses associated with Tornado Cash and centralized exchanges. Chainalysis reported that the laundering operation had used more than 12,000 addresses. ([S2](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/); [S3](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

For Harmony, Elliptic described post-Tornado withdrawal addresses, dormant periods, subsequent Railgun deposits, and deposits into three cryptoasset exchanges. It specifically stated that Binance and Huobi identified, blocked, and seized a portion of the funds. ([S1](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

The wallet evidence supports a network-level linkage because both cases exhibit the same broad sequence: theft wallet or wallets, intermediary wallets, privacy or mixing infrastructure, cross-chain or asset conversion, and eventual exchange exposure. It does not, by itself, establish that every intermediary address was directly controlled by Lazarus Group. Some addresses could have represented service infrastructure, counterparties, exchange deposit addresses, or unrelated users whose funds became commingled.

## Recovery and disruption

Chainalysis reported that more than $30 million in cryptocurrency stolen by North Korean-linked hackers had been seized with the assistance of law enforcement, exchanges, and other industry participants. It characterized the seizures as approximately 10% of the total Ronin theft, subject to differences between the prices at the time of theft and seizure. ([S2](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/))

For Harmony, Elliptic reported that Binance and Huobi blocked and seized a portion of the funds after tracing activity through Railgun and other addresses. The source does not state the exact amount seized from Harmony. ([S1](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

These outcomes demonstrate that laundering through transparent blockchains creates exposure at exchange deposit points even when mixers, bridges, and token swaps are used. The evidence supports the conclusion that operational complexity delayed attribution and recovery but did not eliminate traceability.

## Final findings

The most defensible conclusion is that the Ronin and Harmony thefts were part of a connected Lazarus Group campaign against cryptocurrency infrastructure. The connection is supported by:

- independent public attribution of Ronin to Lazarus Group by OFAC;
- FBI confirmation of the Lazarus attribution for Harmony;
- Elliptic’s identification of Ronin-like laundering patterns in the Harmony case;
- recurring use of Tornado Cash and structured transaction flows;
- use of intermediary wallets and large-scale address networks;
- adaptation to cross-chain DeFi services after sanctions against Tornado Cash; and
- repeated movement of funds toward centralized exchanges, where blocking and seizure were possible.

The evidence does not independently prove the narrower proposition that Lazarus Group and APT38 are identical organizational entities, nor does it identify individual operators. The supplied sources support “Lazarus Group” and “North Korea-linked” terminology, but not a definitive APT38 attribution. The linkage should therefore be expressed as: **Ronin and Harmony were publicly attributed to Lazarus Group, and their laundering patterns show strong operational continuity; an APT38 equivalence is not established by the supplied evidence.**

Cryptocurrency Community Is Making It Difficult for North Korean Hackers To Profit September 8, 2022 | Erin Plante One of the most troubling trends in crypto crime right now is the stunning rise in funds stolen from DeFi protocols , and in particular cross-chain bridges . Much of the value stolen from DeFi protocols can be attributed to bad actors affiliated with North Korea, especially elite hacking units like Lazarus Group. We estimate that so far in 2022, North Korea-linked groups have stolen approximately $1 billion of cryptocurrency from DeFi protocols. But today I had the privilege of joining the Axie Infinity team on stage at AxieCon to deliver some good news: With the help of law enforcement and leading organizations in the cryptocurrency industry, more than $30 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen by North Korean-linked hackers has been seized. This marks the first time ever that cryptocurrency stolen by a North Korean hacking group has been seized, and we’re confident it won’t be the last. These are the results thus far of our investigation following the March 2022 theft of more than $600 million from Ronin Network, a sidechain built for the play-to-earn game Axie Infinity. I am proud to say that the Chainalysis Crypto Incident Response team played a role in these seizures, utilizing advanced tracing techniques to follow stolen funds to cash out points and liaising with law enforcement and industry players to quickly freeze funds. The seizures represent approximately 10% of the total funds stolen from Axie Infinity (accounting for price differences between time stolen and seized), and demonstrate that it is becoming more difficult for bad actors to successfully cash out their ill-gotten crypto gains. We have proven that with the right blockchain analysis tools, world-class investigators and compliance professionals can collaborate to stop even the most sophisticated hackers and launderers. There is still work to be done, but this is a milestone in our efforts to make the cryptocurrency ecosystem safer. So, how did we do it? Here’s what we can share now. How the Ronin Bridge was hacked & the stolen funds were laundered The attack began when the Lazarus Group gained access to five of the nine private keys held by transaction validators for Ronin Network’s cross-chain bridge. They used this majority to approve two transactions, both withdrawals: one for 173,600 ether (ETH) and the other for 25.5 million USD Coin (USDC). They then initiated their laundering process – and Chainalysis began tracing the funds. The laundering of these funds has leveraged over 12,000 different crypto addresses to-date, which demonstrates the hackers’ highly sophisticated laundering capabilities. North Korea’s typical DeFi laundering technique has roughly five stages: Stolen Ether sent to intermediary wallets Ether mixed in batches using Tornado Cash Ether swapped for bitcoin Bitcoin mixed in batches Bitcoin deposited to crypto-to-fiat services for cashout Lazarus Group has replicated this process with large portions of Ronin’s stolen funds. We can visualize it below using Chainalysis Reactor: However, the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) recently sanctioned Tornado Cash for its role in laundering over $455 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Axie Infinity. Since then, Lazarus Group has moved away from the popular Ethereum mixer, instead leveraging DeFi services to chain hop, or switch between several different kinds of cryptocurrencies in a single transaction. Bridges serve an important function to move digital assets between chains and most usage of these platforms is completely legitimate. Lazarus appears to be using bridges in an attempt to obscure source of funds. With Chainalysis tools these cross chain funds movements are easily traced. We can use Chainalysis Storyline to see an example of how Lazarus Group utilized chain-hopping to launder some of the funds stolen from Axie Infinity: Above, we see that the hacker bridged ETH from the Ethereum blockchain to the BNB chain and then swapped that ETH for USDD, which was then bridged to the BitTorrent chain. Lazarus Group carried out hundreds of similar transactions across several blockchains to launder the funds they stole from Axie Infinity, in addition to the more conventional Tornado Cash-based laundering we covered above. Transparency and collaboration are key Cryptocurrency’s transparency is instrumental to investigating hacks like the one suffered by Axie Infinity. Investigators with the right tools can follow the money to understand and disrupt a cybercrime organization’s laundering activities. This would never be possible in traditional financial channels, where money laundering usually involves networks of shell companies and financial institutions in jurisdictions that may not cooperate. Even so, these seizures would not have been possible without collaboration across the public and private sectors. Much of the funds stolen from Axie Infinity remain unspent in cryptocurrency wallets under the hackers’ control. We look forward to continuing to work with the cryptocurrency ecosystem to prevent them and other illicit actors from cashing out their funds. The total value of the stolen cryptoassets at the time of the theft was $540 million. This is the second largest crypto theft of all time. On April 14th, the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new sanctions against the thief's Ethereum address and listed the owner of this address as Lazarus Group – the North Korean state hacking group . The sanctions prohibit US persons and entities from transacting with this address to ensure the state-sponsored group can’t cash out any further funds they continue to hold onto through US-based crypto exchanges. The incident occurred six days before the exploit was announced by Ronin. Amid confusion over the delayed response, it announced that the exploit was only discovered after a 5,000 ETH withdrawal attempt from one of their users failed. At the time of discovery, the stolen funds were worth over $615 million. How the hack unfolded How the hack unfolded According to a postmortem published by Ronin, the theft came as a result of an attacker hacking the “validator nodes”of the Ronin bridge. Funds can be moved out if five of the nine validators approve it. The attacker managed to get hold of the private cryptographic keys belonging to five of the validators, which was enough to steal the cryptoassets. The post mortem claims that “all evidence points to this attack being socially engineered, rather than a technical flaw ”. Laundering the stolen crypto Laundering the stolen crypto Elliptic’s internal analysis indicates that the attacker has managed to launder 18% of their stolen funds as of April 14th. First, the stolen USDC was swapped for ETH through decentralized exchanges (DEXs) to prevent it from being seized. Tokens such as stablecoins are controlled by their issuers, who in some cases can freeze tokens involved in illicit activity. By converting the tokens at DEXs, the hacker avoided the anti-money laundering (AML) and 'know your customer' (KYC) checks performed at centralized exchanges. This is an increasingly common tactic seen in hacks of this type, as described in Elliptic’s recent report: “ DeFi: Risk, Regulation, and the Rise of DeCrime ” . However, the attacker then began laundering $16.7 million worth of ETH through three centralized exchanges. This strategy is uncommon for typical DeFi exploits given these exchanges’ AML obligations, though it has been observed more often in past Lazarus group-affiliated exploits. As the affected exchanges publicly announced that they would work with law enforcement to establish their identity, the attacker changed their laundering strategy to instead make use of Tornado Cash – a popular smart contract-based mixer on the Ethereum blockchain. Ongoing transactions have so far sent $80.3 million worth of ETH through Tornado Cash. Destination of $107 million ETH of the stolen $540 million ETH & USDC. The attacker’s blockchain activity shows that another $9.7 million worth of ETH is in intermediary wallets prepared to be laundered, most likely also through Tornado Cash. This leaves a considerable $433 million remaining in the attacker’s original wallet. Elliptic investigators are tracking these stolen funds, and have labelled the addresses associated to this attacker in our systems – ensuring that our clients will be alerted if they receive any of these funds. How the Lazarus Group is laundering its funds. Source: Elliptic Forensics . Lazarus Group’s targeting of crypto entities Lazarus Group’s targeting of crypto entities Lazarus Group refers to a group of North Korean state hackers who have been targeting crypto entities since at least 2017. Until 2021, the majority of this activity was directed towards centralized exchanges located in South Korea or elsewhere in Asia. However, within the past year the group’s attention has turned to DeFi services. While the service that was attacked in this instance – Ronin Network’s bridge – is decentralized, the creators of the network Sky Mavis are located in Vietnam. It is somewhat unsurprising that this attack has been attributed to North Korea. Many features of the attack mirrored the method used by Lazarus Group in previous high-profile attacks, including the location of the victim, the attack method (believed to have involved social engineering) and the laundering pattern utilized by the group after the event. Many commentators believe that cryptoassets stolen by Lazarus Group are used to fund the state’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs. With recent reports that North Korea may be again preparing for nuclear testing, today’s sanctions activity highlights the importance of ensuring that Lazarus Group is not able to successfully launder the proceeds of these attacks. The announcement confirms Elliptic’s previous attribution of the $100 million hack to North Korea, which we were the first to identify after numerous similarities were observed with Lazarus’ past blockchain laundering patterns. This is a preview of our upcoming briefing note into tracing the stolen funds from the Harmony Horizon Hack to North Korea, including the demixing of the funds through Tornado Cash and Railgun. Horizon – a cross-chain bridge servicing the Harmony blockchain – was exploited on June 24th 2022 for $99.7 million. Concerns had previously been raised that the bridge was over-centralized, meaning that it was particularly vulnerable to social engineering attacks – a common attack vector for the Lazarus Group. Similar issues resulted in the criminal organization stealing over $540 million from another cross-chain bridge called Ronin earlier in March 2022. After stealing the funds from Horizon, the Lazarus Group then programmatically structured transactions through Tornado Cash, which is a decentralized Ethereum-based mixer. Elliptic researchers identified that the laundering methods employed mirrored those the Lazarus Group had used when attempting to conceal funds from the Ronin Bridge hack, which had also been sent through Tornado Cash. US sanctions US sanctions Tornado Cash was subsequently sanctioned by the US Treasury in August 2022, with Secretary of State Anthony Blinken citing its prolific use by the Lazarus Group to launder funds from its past hacks. Elliptic’s research suggests that the Lazarus Group sent more than $555 million through Tornado Cash from these hacks, including more than $468 million from the Ronin hack and $96 million from the Harmony hack. This North Korea-linked activity accounts for approximately 5.8% of the nearly $9 billion in total funds sent through the Tornado Cash mixer to date. Elliptic has traced the stolen funds from the Horizon hack through Tornado Cash. Our forthcoming briefing note will break down the methodology we used and how it ultimately aided the eventual attribution of the exploit to the Lazarus Group. The post-Tornado withdrawals were initially placed into several addresses, where they remained dormant until January 2023. Elliptic has previously identified Railgun as a prime alternative to Tornado Cash following sanctions against the latter. You can read more about Railgun – and other Ethereum-based privacy-enhancing solutions – in our Tornado Cash Alternatives Briefing note . Railgun Railgun Elliptic’s research suggests that a significant portion of funds – estimated at around 70% – that has been sent through Railgun to date are funds from the Harmony hack. This suggests that since the OFAC sanctions on Tornado Cash, North Korea may be turning to lower obfuscating services as an alternative. However, the fact that funds from the Harmony hack comprised such a substantial volume of the Ether passing through Railgun renders the mixing ineffective. As an analogy, imagine if you threw five pennies into a jar full of 100 pennies, it would be extremely difficult for someone to determine which pennies were yours. However, if you threw 70 pennies into a jar with only 30 other pennies in it, then there would be a higher chance of linking those 70 specific pennies back to you. Mixers work in a similar way: when the anonymity set – or volume of other funds in the mixer is low – it makes the mixer less effective at concealing disproportionately large funds transfers. On-chain data shows that after sending the funds through Railgun, the Lazarus Group has since deposited funds into three cryptoasset exchanges. Two, namely Binance and Huobi, have announced that they have identified, blocked and seized a portion of the funds. This case demonstrates the importance of cryptoasset exchanges utlizing blockchain analytics solutions to identify transactions involving mixing services abused by sanctioned actors such as North Korea. Elliptic’s Holistic wallet and transaction screening solutions enable our customers to identify and block transactions involving these mixing services, including where there may be sanctions implications - such as links to North Korean perpetrated hacks. Cryptocurrency Community Is Making It Difficult for North Korean Hackers To Profit September 8, 2022 | Erin Plante One of the most troubling trends in crypto crime right now is the stunning rise in funds stolen from DeFi protocols , and in particular cross-chain bridges . Much of the value stolen from DeFi protocols can be attributed to bad actors affiliated with North Korea, especially elite hacking units like Lazarus Group. We estimate that so far in 2022, North Korea-linked groups have stolen approximately $1 billion of cryptocurrency from DeFi protocols. But today I had the privilege of joining the Axie Infinity team on stage at AxieCon to deliver some good news: With the help of law enforcement and leading organizations in the cryptocurrency industry, more than $30 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen by North Korean-linked hackers has been seized. This marks the first time ever that cryptocurrency stolen by a North Korean hacking group has been seized, and we’re confident it won’t be the last. These are the results thus far of our investigation following the March 2022 theft of more than $600 million from Ronin Network, a sidechain built for the play-to-earn game Axie Infinity. I am proud to say that the Chainalysis Crypto Incident Response team played a role in these seizures, utilizing advanced tracing techniques to follow stolen funds to cash out points and liaising with law enforcement and industry players to quickly freeze funds. The seizures represent approximately 10% of the total funds stolen from Axie Infinity (accounting for price differences between time stolen and seized), and demonstrate that it is becoming more difficult for bad actors to successfully cash out their ill-gotten crypto gains. We have proven that with the right blockchain analysis tools, world-class investigators and compliance professionals can collaborate to stop even the most sophisticated hackers and launderers. There is still work to be done, but this is a milestone in our efforts to make the cryptocurrency ecosystem safer. So, how did we do it? Here’s what we can share now. How the Ronin Bridge was hacked & the stolen funds were laundered The attack began when the Lazarus Group gained access to five of the nine private keys held by transaction validators for Ronin Network’s cross-chain bridge. They used this majority to approve two transactions, both withdrawals: one for 173,600 ether (ETH) and the other for 25.5 million USD Coin (USDC). They then initiated their laundering process – and Chainalysis began tracing the funds. The laundering of these funds has leveraged over 12,000 different crypto addresses to-date, which demonstrates the hackers’ highly sophisticated laundering capabilities. North Korea’s typical DeFi laundering technique has roughly five stages: Stolen Ether sent to intermediary wallets Ether mixed in batches using Tornado Cash Ether swapped for bitcoin Bitcoin mixed in batches Bitcoin deposited to crypto-to-fiat services for cashout Lazarus Group has replicated this process with large portions of Ronin’s stolen funds. We can visualize it below using Chainalysis Reactor: However, the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) recently sanctioned Tornado Cash for its role in laundering over $455 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Axie Infinity. Since then, Lazarus Group has moved away from the popular Ethereum mixer, instead leveraging DeFi services to chain hop, or switch between several different kinds of cryptocurrencies in a single transaction. Bridges serve an important function to move digital assets between chains and most usage of these platforms is completely legitimate. Lazarus appears to be using bridges in an attempt to obscure source of funds. With Chainalysis tools these cross chain funds movements are easily traced. We can use Chainalysis Storyline to see an example of how Lazarus Group utilized chain-hopping to launder some of the funds stolen from Axie Infinity: Above, we see that the hacker bridged ETH from the Ethereum blockchain to the BNB chain and then swapped that ETH for USDD, which was then bridged to the BitTorrent chain. Lazarus Group carried out hundreds of similar transactions across several blockchains to launder the funds they stole from Axie Infinity, in addition to the more conventional Tornado Cash-based laundering we covered above. Transparency and collaboration are key Cryptocurrency’s transparency is instrumental to investigating hacks like the one suffered by Axie Infinity. Investigators with the right tools can follow the money to understand and disrupt a cybercrime organization’s laundering activities. This would never be possible in traditional financial channels, where money laundering usually involves networks of shell companies and financial institutions in jurisdictions that may not cooperate. Even so, these seizures would not have been possible without collaboration across the public and private sectors. Much of the funds stolen from Axie Infinity remain unspent in cryptocurrency wallets under the hackers’ control. We look forward to continuing to work with the cryptocurrency ecosystem to prevent them and other illicit actors from cashing out their funds. FAQs All your questions, answered Community Webinars Newsroom Partners Success story Global crypto exchange realizes $3.1M efficiency gain with Elliptic Global crypto exchange realizes $3.1M efficiency gain with Elliptic Uncover the story Company & Careers About Elliptic Security & Trust Careers Contact Sign in Get a demo Insights & research Mar 29, 2022 DeFi North Korea’s Lazarus Group identified as exploiters behind $540 million Ronin bridge heist North Korea’s Lazarus Group identified as exploiters behind $540 million Ronin bridge heist By Elliptic Intel [Update: this blog has been updated to reflect US sanctions announced against the Ronin Bridge Exploiter’s Ethereum address on April 14th 2022] On March 29th, the Ronin Network announced that 173,600 Ether (ETH) and 25.5 million USD Coins had been stolen from the Ronin cross-chain bridge six days earlier. The total value of the stolen cryptoassets at the time of the theft was $540 million. This is the second largest crypto theft of all time. On April 14th, the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new sanctions against the thief's Ethereum address and listed the owner of this address as Lazarus Group – the North Korean state hacking group . The sanctions prohibit US persons and entities from transacting with this address to ensure the state-sponsored group can’t cash out any further funds they continue to hold onto through US-based crypto exchanges. The incident occurred six days before the exploit was announced by Ronin. Amid confusion over the delayed response, it announced that the exploit was only discovered after a 5,000 ETH withdrawal attempt from one of their users failed. At the time of discovery, the stolen funds were worth over $615 million. How the hack unfolded How the hack unfolded According to a postmortem published by Ronin, the theft came as a result of an attacker hacking the “validator nodes”of the Ronin bridge. Funds can be moved out if five of the nine validators approve it. The attacker managed to get hold of the private cryptographic keys belonging to five of the validators, which was enough to steal the cryptoassets. The post mortem claims that “all evidence points to this attack being socially engineered, rather than a technical flaw ”. Laundering the stolen crypto Laundering the stolen crypto Elliptic’s internal analysis indicates that the attacker has managed to launder 18% of their stolen funds as of April 14th. First, the stolen USDC was swapped for ETH through decentralized exchanges (DEXs) to prevent it from being seized. Tokens such as stablecoins are controlled by their issuers, who in some cases can freeze tokens involved in illicit activity. By converting the tokens at DEXs, the hacker avoided the anti-money laundering (AML) and 'know your customer' (KYC) checks performed at centralized exchanges. This is an increasingly common tactic seen in hacks of this type, as described in Elliptic’s recent report: “ DeFi: Risk, Regulation, and the Rise of DeCrime ” . However, the attacker then began laundering $16.7 million worth of ETH through three centralized exchanges. This strategy is uncommon for typical DeFi exploits given these exchanges’ AML obligations, though it has been observed more often in past Lazarus group-affiliated exploits. As the affected exchanges publicly announced that they would work with law enforcement to establish their identity, the attacker changed their laundering strategy to instead make use of Tornado Cash – a popular smart contract-based mixer on the Ethereum blockchain. Ongoing transactions have so far sent $80.3 million worth of ETH through Tornado Cash. Destination of $107 million ETH of the stolen $540 million ETH & USDC. The attacker’s blockchain activity shows that another $9.7 million worth of ETH is in intermediary wallets prepared to be laundered, most likely also through Tornado Cash. This leaves a considerable $433 million remaining in the attacker’s original wallet. Elliptic investigators are tracking these stolen funds, and have labelled the addresses associated to this attacker in our systems – ensuring that our clients will be alerted if they receive any of these funds. How the Lazarus Group is laundering its funds. Source: Elliptic Forensics . Lazarus Group’s targeting of crypto entities Lazarus Group’s targeting of crypto entities Lazarus Group refers to a group of North Korean state hackers who have been targeting crypto entities since at least 2017. Until 2021, the majority of this activity was directed towards centralized exchanges located in South Korea or elsewhere in Asia. However, within the past year the group’s attention has turned to DeFi services. While the service that was attacked in this instance – Ronin Network’s bridge – is decentralized, the creators of the network Sky Mavis are located in Vietnam. It is somewhat unsurprising that this attack has been attributed to North Korea. Many features of the attack mirrored the method used by Lazarus Group in previous high-profile attacks, including the location of the victim, the attack method (believed to have involved social engineering) and the laundering pattern utilized by the group after the event. Many commentators believe that cryptoassets stolen by Lazarus Group are used to fund the state’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs. With recent reports that North Korea may be again preparing for nuclear testing, today’s sanctions activity highlights the importance of ensuring that Lazarus Group is not able to successfully launder the proceeds of these attacks.
